items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 7, 2026
items.excerpt: 07 November 2026• Update: 07 November 2026 HAMILTON, Canada Here's a rundown of all the news you need to know for Saturday, including Russian President Vladimir Putin confirming that the next round of Russia-US-Ukraine talks will begin Tuesday in Abu Dhabi; US President Donald Trump naming Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff to replace Susie Wiles and saying he plans Cabinet changes after the midterm election losses; and bomb threats targeting flights, airports and media outlets in at least five European countries. Russian President Vladimir Putin confirmed that the next round of talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine is expected to begin next Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, with Russian state media reporting the talks would last two days. Putin said he invited members of the Russian delegation, headed by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky, to a UN Security Council meeting ahead of the negotiations, Tass reported. US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff previously said the parties intend to discuss security guarantees, de-escalation, humanitarian issues and further steps toward a peaceful settlement. - Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff, says he plans Cabinet changes after midterm losses Trump announced that Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff starting Monday, while Wiles moves to the Trump political operation. “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves,” Trump told reporters, saying he “wanted to make a change.” Trump said he plans to make changes to his Cabinet after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections earlier this week, telling CBS News’ 60 Minutes, “I do, yeah. Little bit,” when asked whether he plans to fire anyone, in an interview set to air Sunday. - Bomb threats target flights, media outlets in at least 5 European countries Bomb threats targeted flights, airports and media organizations in at least five European countries, prompting security inspections and evacuations, according to authorities and the media. Two aircraft departing from London and Brussels were diverted to Sofia and landed safely, while Czech police inspected nine aircraft following anonymous threats against four arrivals and five departures at Prague Airport. The French prime minister’s office said four aircraft flying over French territory received threats and all landed safely, and Copenhagen Police completed security checks at the city’s airport. Several Irish media organizations, including RTE, evacuated their premises after a threatening email was sent to broadcasters and news outlets in Ireland and Britain, with Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin calling the threats “worrying.” The incidents followed similar threats Thursday against at least 18 flights across Europe.

items.excerpt: House Democrats will start their majority focused on boosting healthcare and ending the Iran war WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democratic leaders are placing an early emphasis on healthcare as they discuss their immediate priorities upon the swearing in of a new Congress on Jan. 3. Early votes in the House next year are expected to focus on boosting Medicaid and restoring an enhanced tax subsidy for Affordable Care Act health plans. Democrats are also promising early votes on legislation to stop the war with Iran and to reverse some of President Donald Trump’s trade tariffs. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries is in line to become the next House speaker and he's promising Democrats will “get out of the gate fast.” Trump’s grip on his party is in question as Republicans reel from the midterm wipeout WASHINGTON (AP) — Republicans are reeling from the midterm elections and facing a crisis. Ron DeSantis, the Florida governor, calls it an “extinction-level event” for the party. Ted Cruz, the Texas senator, compares it to a “Watergate-level repudiation.” The party is divided on how to move forward. Some want to return to fiscal conservatism. Others suggest embracing President Donald Trump’s politics. Trump's role in shaping the party's future is a key question. GOP infighting is expected to intensify, with leadership battles and policy decisions looming. The party must also address its appeal to younger voters and minorities to regain lost ground. ... WASHINGTON (AP) — Young voters voted overwhelmingly for Democrats in the midterm elections, driven by economic concerns and disillusionment with President ... Gunman opens fire in Polish city of Krakow, killing 5 people and injuring at least 12 KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — A gunman opened fire in Krakow, Poland, killing five people and wounding more than a dozen. The attack happened Saturday afternoon in Main Square, a popular tourist spot. Police say the gunman aimed at random people as he drove into the area. Officers are among the wounded. The perpetrator was shot and wounded during a confrontation with police. Images show police and ambulances covering the scene, with a medical helicopter landing in the square. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk says police are investigating. Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. The U.S. ambassador expressed solidarity with Poland. Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Drone and missile explosions wounded at least nine people across Ukraine Saturday, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States. Negotiators from the three countries are set to meet Tuesday in Abu Dhabi to discuss ending the war. This will be the fourth round of negotiations brokered by the Trump administration. Western governments are seeking a new formula to break the impasse, though territorial and security issues remain unresolved. The missiles also closed traffic on a Kyiv bridge and caused power and water outages. Meanwhile, recovery efforts continue in Komyshuvakha after a deadly attack there killed at least 55 people.

items.title: Daly Says Fed May Need More Rate Increases as Inflation Persists | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: By Miriam Hart Nov 7, 2026, 9:43 AM UTC Updated Nov 7, 2026, 9:43 AM UTC 2 min read ... U.S. wage growth remained below the latest annual inflation reading, and San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank President Mary Daly said the Fed may need to raise rates again as price pressures persist. Daly made the assessment in a Nov. 6 interview with CNBC. She said officials would consider incoming economic information before deciding whether or when to act. “My expectation is we’re going to have to tighten policy further,” she said. Daly did not set a timetable or specify the size of a possible increase. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that employers added 165,000 jobs in October and unemployment edged down to 4.1%. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% from a year earlier that month, while the consumer price index increased 3.7% year over year in September. Daly welcomed the job gains but said inflation continued to weigh on household finances. She said people were still finding work and spending, while pay gains failed to keep pace with prices. She described labor conditions as steady but not unusually strong, and said inflation’s persistence concerned her more than economic growth. Daly also said inflation had remained high for almost six years, with its burden spreading across households. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised its target range for the federal funds rate by 0.25 percentage point in September, to 3.75% to 4%. On Oct. 28, it left the range unchanged and said additional information would guide its policy stance. Daly said she supported both decisions and continued to favor a gradual approach. Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin also expects further increases may be needed, CNBC reported, though he has not identified when. The next report on October CPI is scheduled for Nov. 10, and the FOMC’s next meeting is set for Dec. 8-9.

items.title: President Donald Trump Just Proclaimed That "Inflation Is Way Down," but Federal Reserve Economists Have a Different Take | The Motley Fool
items.excerpt: ## Federal Reserve economists have bad news for Trump (and Wall Street): inflation is rising However, inflation isn't "way down," as Donald Trump has proclaimed. Though annualized inflation is well below its four-decade high of 9.1% in June 2022, the reported annualized rate of 3.7% for September is nearly double the FOMC's long-term target of 2%. Keep in mind that consumer prices are expected to rise when the U.S. economy is expanding. If businesses are firing on all cylinders, they should possess some degree of pricing power over their goods and services. The issue is that annualized inflation has moved well above what Warsh and the FOMC would consider "modest," and two of the president's policies are mostly to blame. ... Despite Trump's recent claim that tariffs don't cause inflation, three New York Federal Reserve economists writing for Liberty Street Economics examined the inflationary effects of the president's 2025 tariffs on consumer prices. In their report ("How Fast Do Tariffs Pass Through into Consumer Prices?"), the authors estimated that Trump's tariffs raised goods price inflation by 2.9 percentage points by February 2026. Conversely, goods prices would have declined had Trump not imposed tariffs!

items.title: Musalem says inflation concern persists, expectations anchored
items.excerpt: Last updated: 7 November 2026 03:04 Enver Adıgüzel - Editor and Publisher 9 minutes ago St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said people remain concerned about inflation at the current level. He said inflation expectations remain anchored. The Fed, he said, must return inflation to 2% on a timely basis. Contents - Energy shocks and AI spending - Communication and policy transmission ## Energy shocks and AI spending Musalem attributed the current excess inflation to energy shocks and the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure. He said consumption and investment are growing fast on an optimistic outlook. He argued that AI will bring much higher productivity, and that data center construction is adding to strong demand. Musalem’s remarks point to demand as well as energy costs as the source of the pressure. ## Communication and policy transmission Musalem said clear Fed communication helps policy move through the economy more smoothly. items.excerpt: Published November 7, 2026 Updated November 7, 2026 07:01am By Reuters NEW YORK: The US dollar index jumped on Friday and was on pace for its biggest daily percentage gain in seven weeks as it extended gains after a stronger-than-expected US payrolls report. The Labor Department said US nonfarm payrolls jumped by 165,000 jobs last month, topping the 65,000 estimate of economists polled by Reuters, after an upwardly revised 60,000 gain in September, while the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1 percent. The report gives the Federal Reserve latitude to continue to hike interest rates, and market expectations for an increase of at least 25 basis points at the central bank’s December meeting moved back up towards 80 percent in the wake of the report, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. ... items.title: Risk of Iran war escalation remains high despite Democratic election sweep
items.excerpt: Published Sat, Nov 7 2026 8:03 AM EST Spencer Kimball@spencekimball Key Points - Crude oil prices sold off this week as investors hoped the Democratic victory in the U.S. midterm elections would force an end to the Iran war. - But tensions remain high in the Middle East, with the Gulf states still bracing for escalation, analysts say. - The Democrats' options are limited until they take control of Congress in January. - And President Donald Trump has reiterated that he will not allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon. The U.S. and Iran are careening toward renewed war despite growing hopes this week that the Democrats' decisive midterm election victory will bring the conflict to an end, analysts say. Crude oil prices fell more than 16% over the last five trading days after Vice President JD Vance publicly blamed the Republicans' stinging loss on the war. Vance's remarks raised questions about whether there is still support within the administration to continue the conflict with Iran. The Democrats plan to use their comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress to pass a war powers resolution that demands President Donald Trump end the war. But tensions in the Middle East have not eased since the election, and the Democrats aren't sworn in until January, the analysts say. ... ### Price risk Crude oil prices will vault above $100 a barrel again in response to renewed fighting, said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan and a former energy advisor to President George W. Bush. Brent crude, the international benchmark, was trading above $97 on Friday while U.S. crude was around $90. ... The risk of war is still alive, especially since Trump doesn't face anymore future elections, said Amos Hochstein, a former energy advisor to President Joe Biden. Gasoline, diesel and jet fuel prices would all surge as a consequence, Hochstein told CNBC's " Power Lunch" Friday.

items.title: Fed’s Williams says energy prices have already peaked despite new Iran fighting | Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide
items.excerpt: in World Economy News 11/07/2026 Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said today he does not expect a sustained rise in energy prices for the rest of the year, despite renewed conflict in the Middle East. Williams told a conference at his bank that market expectations for oil prices to decline over the next six to 12 months remain reasonable. He said the fundamentals suggest energy prices are likely around their peak and should come down over time. The Fed official said inflation remains “far too high” and that monetary policy is focused on how energy prices impact inflation. Williams added that artificial intelligence investment is currently driving inflation, though he expects AI to become a positive supply shock in the longer term. His base case sees broader AI use boosting productivity. Williams said the Fed is actively debating scenarios around inflation and remains committed to bringing inflation back to 2%. He stressed the importance of looking at underlying inflation factors rather than just specific measures, noting that government technical changes could better reconcile differences between PCE inflation and CPI. The New York Fed president said monetary policy needs to remain data dependent. He described the labor market as very stable. Williams noted that uncertainty remains about the longer-term neutral rate and that the Fed minutes captured a “collective reaction function.”

items.title: Live updates: Trump taps Stephen Miller as new chief of staff
items.excerpt: Updated November 07, 2026, 11:06 AM EST By NBC News ## What to know today - WILES OUT: President Donald Trump announced Friday that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles would be leaving her role this week and would be replaced by deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. - STILL COUNTING: Votes are still being counted in the shockingly close Alaska and Mississippi Senate races. Democratic candidates Mary Peltola and Scott Colom continue to narrowly lead their Republican opponents, GOP Sens. Dan Sullivan and Cindy Hyde-Smith, respectively. - CALIFORNIA BALLOTS: The Justice Department moved to dismiss its bid to separate more than 20,000 California ballots it alleged were cast by noncitizens. California officials had argued that the list was out of date and included legitimate voters. 49m ago / 11:06 AM EST ## Trump floats being kind to Democrats in exchange for bipartisan deals In a new clip released ahead of his full "60 Minutes" interview airing Sunday, Trump said he could go six months without insulting Democrats if it meant getting a deal done. Asked by CBS News' Ross Douthat about newly elected Texas Democratic Sen. James Talarico expressing interest in working with him on immigration, Trump noted that other Democrats had also expressed a willingness to cooperate. Trump acknowledged calling Talarico “Talafreako” during the campaign as well as referring to many Democrats as “Dumbocrats.” On whether he could refrain from insults for six months to secure a deal, Trump responded, “Very easily.” The president's comments come days after Democrats flipped the House and Senate in the midterm elections, with NBC News projecting Democrats could have 259 House seats next year, far beyond the 218 needed for a majority. In the Senate, Democratic candidates also flipped Senate seats in South Carolina, Texas, Maine and Ohio, cementing a Democratic majority in Congress' upper chamber. ## Americans voted for change. Trump, so far, is delivering the same. Voters sent a thunderous message Tuesday night that they’re angry about the nation’s direction under President Donald Trump and want to see more attention paid to high gas and grocery prices. Since then, Trump has shown scant signs that he’s listening. The day after millions of Americans repudiated the president and his party, Trump instead turned to renovations. He showed up at his ballroom construction site and offered a play-by-play as workers hoisted a steel beam to the roof. He also posted on social media that the Senate needs to pass a bill that would make daylight saving time year-round, something that doesn’t make the list of issues that voters deem top of mind.
